content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'gnashing of teeth' (nearly always paired with 'weeping') symbolizes the extreme anguish, despair, and suffering of those who are excluded from God's kingdom and consigned to final judgment or hell. It functions as a stock formula in Jesus' teaching for the conscious misery and regret of the condemned — the pain of eschatological loss.", "primary_basis": ["Matthew 8:12", "Matthew 13:42", "Matthew 13:50", "Matthew 22:13", "Matthew 24:51", "Matthew 25:30", "Luke 13:28"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Gnashing of teeth as an expression of rage, hostility, or defiant anger rather than sorrow. In the Old Testament and Acts, gnashing teeth consistently signals fury directed at the righteous (the wicked gnash at the psalmist; the Sanhedrin gnashes at Stephen). Some interpreters therefore read the Gospel formula as the condemned raging against God rather than merely grieving.", "basis": ["Psalm 35:16", "Psalm 37:12", "Psalm 112:10", "Job 16:9", "Lamentations 2:16", "Acts 7:54"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Gnashing of teeth as remorse and self-reproach — the condemned grinding their teeth in bitter regret over lost opportunity, emphasized in some patristic and devotional readings (e.g., contrast between seeing the patriarchs in the kingdom while being cast out in Luke 13:28).", "basis": ["Luke 13:28", "Psalm 112:10"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "A conditionalist/annihilationist reading: the weeping and gnashing occur at the moment of exclusion and judgment (the 'casting out') rather than describing an unending conscious state, so the phrase does not by itself prove eternal conscious torment.", "basis": ["Matthew 8:12", "Matthew 13:42", "Psalm 112:10 (the wicked 'melts away' / perishes after gnashing)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "A literal-physical reading tied to fiery torment (teeth chattering or grinding from pain, sometimes paired in older interpretation with 'outer darkness' as literal cold and dark), found in some medieval and popular-literalist treatments.", "basis": ["Matthew 13:42", "Matthew 22:13"], "prominence": "rare"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is broad, recognizable consensus that the phrase is a fixed Matthean/Lukan formula describing the state of the finally excluded, with anguish/despair as the dominant gloss. The main live scholarly and homiletical debate is whether the gesture connotes grief and regret or anger and defiance, since the Old Testament background (Psalms, Job, Lamentations) and Acts 7:54 uniformly use gnashing for rage. Many commentators combine the two, taking weeping as sorrow and gnashing as fury or bitter frustration. Disagreements about the duration or literalness of the state reflect wider disputes over the nature of hell rather than over the phrase's basic symbolic force."}
